title: not-self
hook: not-self — who's actually in there? (the question, not the answer)
tomorrow: a word for wishing well on people you don't like

segments.voice: Yesterday: anicca, impermanence, the first mark. Your line was this passes. Today, the third mark, and the question under day seven's flame. Day fourteen.

Try this. Say the word I, and then try to point to it. A finger usually goes to the chest. But is that it? The body at six is not the body now. Opinions change. Taste in music changes. A mood can turn twice before lunch. So who's the I that stayed the same through all of that? It's an old question. The Buddha asked it too, and his answer is well known and often misunderstood. Today we're taking the question, not the answer.
screen: `SAY "I", THEN POINT TO IT.` → `BODY, OPINIONS, MOODS, ALL CHANGING.` → `WHO'S ACTUALLY IN THERE?`

segments.voice: Anatta. Atta means self, the unchanging core, the owner. An-atta: not-self. It's the third mark of existence, after anicca and dukkha. Here's how the Buddha is remembered teaching it, to the same five companions from the deer park; tradition counts it as his second discourse. He goes through what a person is made of. The texts count five heaps: the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness. And he asks about each one. Is the body permanent or impermanent? Impermanent. Is what's impermanent something you can rest on, or does it wobble? It wobbles. Then is it right to say of it: this is mine, this is what I am, this is my self? No. And he goes through all five the same way. It's not a lecture. It's a series of questions. Look, and see. Another discourse keeps the question open in a different way. A wanderer asks the Buddha straight out: is there a self? The Buddha is silent. Is there no self? Silent again. Later he explains to his attendant Ananda that either answer would have led the man into a wrong view. Some teachers say anatta is less a doctrine to hold than a way of looking: don't cling to anything as me or mine, and see what happens. Buddhist schools talk about this in different ways. Theravada teachers stress the five heaps and the practice of seeing them as not-self. Mahayana teachers speak of emptiness, and some schools of a buddha-nature in every being. Who's in there? Keep the question open.
screen: `ANATTA — NOT-SELF.` · `FIVE HEAPS, EACH ONE QUESTIONED.` · `IS THERE A SELF? SILENCE.` · `A WAY OF LOOKING.` · then, large: `WHO'S IN THERE?`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and look. Notice a sensation: is it you, or something happening? Notice a thought passing: did you choose it, or did it just arrive? Notice a feeling. Don't answer the question. Don't decide anything. Just keep looking, gently, at whatever shows up, and let the question stay open.
Anatta. Not-self, the third mark: nothing in the five heaps can be held as me, mine, or my self. A question to keep looking into. Fourteenth word.
Your line: look. Two weeks, fourteen words. Next week turns to the heart: friendliness, compassion, good company. Day fourteen, done.

screen: `DAY 14 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A WORD FOR WISHING WELL ON PEOPLE YOU DON'T LIKE.`

howItsDone: Buddhists explore anatta through meditation, observing body, feelings and thoughts without identifying with them, and through study; Theravada teaching centers on the five aggregates, while Mahayana schools also teach it through emptiness.

match.prompt: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
pairs: what a person is made of, questioned

myth: anatta means Buddhists believe you don't exist
it asks whether anything in you can be held as a lasting self. it questions what gets clung to as 'me', not whether you're here.
the Buddha taught anatta through a series of questions
is it permanent? does it wobble? is it right to call it my self?
when asked directly 'is there a self?' the Buddha said no
he was silent, and later said either answer would have misled the man.

fork.setup: a wanderer asks the Buddha directly: is there a self? what does the Buddha do?
fork.reveal: he's silent, both times. afterward he tells Ananda that a yes or a no would have led the man astray. neither answer would have helped him.

original.note: Pali: not-self. an (not) + attā (self). Sanskrit: anātman.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists say you don't exist.
what it means: nothing you're made of, body, feelings, thoughts, can be held as a permanent me. keep looking.

what a scholar hears: anattā, taught in the Anattalakkhana Sutta (SN 22.59) through the five khandhas; in the Ananda Sutta (SN 44.10) the Buddha stays silent when Vacchagotta asks whether there is a self.

sources.ref: Ananda Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 44.10): the Buddha's silence
